headline: RBA likely to pause after this 4th hike; further back-to-back moves hard to defend given risk of rapid economic rollover
reasoning: Flanagan argues there are an unusually large number of important variables at play. Higher oil prices are contractionary in themselves, compounding the impact of rate hikes on discretionary spending. He believes the RBA has enough cover to pause after this hike, as consumer confidence is already very weak and inflation expectations are unlikely to become unhinged if they hold in November. He notes the RBA historically does not hike back-to-back at cycle end, and reversing course quickly in early 2024 would be difficult to defend.
quote: I just think the hurdle that they're well aware that and Michelle Bull talks a lot about not wanting to do it on the, you know, household sector, not wanting to have to do it but having no choice but to do it. So I think they're going to want to be really justified in doing it because the last thing they want to do is go now back to back in November, then we do see things roll over quickly and then we're looking at February, May next year of reversing course. I think that would be wouldn't be an easy move to defend. I know they've got the flexibility to finesse and go up and down, but you kind of want to if you can. headline: David Flanagan sees peak RBA rates as likely but oil prices remain the clear and present danger to the inflation outlook
reasoning: Flanagan believes it is likely Australia has seen peak rates but flags oil as the key residual risk. He notes the RBA's May SMP assumed Brent at just over $100/barrel, now revised down to $95, with an assumption of ~$80 by year-end settling in the mid-70s. He argues this is a rosy assumption and even a brief spike back to $100 could materially knock the inflation forecast. He views the RBA's hawkish tone as apt and sees no reason for the central bank to ease up at this stage.
